docs.title: Rage Tools VI
docs.text:
Reverse engineering of GTA VI / Leonida RPF9 archives, with the long-term goal of enumerating every stored entry and decoding the bytes behind it.

Documentation map

This site is the navigable model of the project. The append-only research record is investigation.md and the live check/todo list is plan.md at the repository root. The diagrams below are the UML/system view that ties those files together.

docs.title: First milestone — met
docs.text:
One decoded record independently predicts the exact byte range of a payload that has already been checksum-verified.

The core_bvh4 descriptor is that record. A decoded 208-byte descriptor carries the entry's exact payload size at +0xa0, pairs with the immediately following stream, and that stream's decoded bytes beyond the declared size are zero — verified on 260 re-decoded samples. Applied across the archive, it yields 188,298 entries across 14 archives, whose boundaries are payload-derived and whose count matches the declared index in 1,253 of 1,261 core_bvh4 packs.

New here? Start with From first principles. The result list is in Findings.

docs.title: Sibling: the GPU layer
docs.text:
The archive work stops at stored bytes. What the GPU does with them is a separate project, kept in its own repository and included here as a submodule:

Path What it does rdna2-spirv/ Generic AMD RDNA2 (GFX10.x) decompiler — machine code to SPIR-V, with decoder agreement against LLVM, golden buffer tests, and exact pixel tests on a software Vulkan backend

Its method, evidence, and open gaps are recorded there, in its own plan.md and investigation.md. Clone with --recurse-submodules to get it.

docs.title: From first principles
docs.text: This page builds the method up from nothing: what the data is, what can be observe, and how each observation leads to the next. No prior knowledge of the game or the format is assumed. Terms are defined the first time they appear.

docs.title: 0. The problem
docs.text:
A game ships its data inside a few very large archive files (.rpf). To mod, audit, or study the game you need to know what is inside them: the entries, their names, where their bytes live, and how those bytes are encoded.

Our goal, stated precisely:

Enumerate every archive entry, locate its stored bytes, and extract it with the correct decoding.

The archives are binary and undocumented. There is no header comment that says "this is the table of contents and here is its entry format". So everything below is inference from bytes, and every claim has to be checkable.

docs.title: 1. What an archive is
docs.text:
An RPF9 archive is a container: a header, three metadata regions, a payload area, and a trailer.

flowchart LR
    H["Header<br/>0x60 bytes"] --> A["Front A<br/>names / paths"]
    A --> B["Front B<br/>entry table"]
    B --> P["Payload<br/>the actual files"]
    P --> T["Trailer<br/>end-of-pack records"]
Region Purpose Readable Header sizes and pointers for the rest yes — every field is now code-confirmed Buffer A header, four sections, then one record per entry the layout yes; the section contents are unidentified Buffer B one fixed-stride record per entry the size law yes (align16(N × stride)); the records are unidentified Payload files, mostly zlib-compressed yes, and verifiable Trailer per-pack records no

The bytes of the two metadata buffers look uniformly random, and no 32-bit or 64-bit hash of any known name appears in them. The executable's loader copies them verbatim — so if a transform exists it lives in the stream's Read, not in the archive layer. That nuance matters less than the practical consequence, which has not changed: contents are reconstructed from the payload, and the metadata only as a cross-check.

docs.title: 2. What can be trusted: checksums
docs.text:
The payload is mostly zlib streams: a compressed block that begins with a recognisable header and ends with a checksum (Adler-32) of the decompressed data.

That gives something rare in reverse engineering, a self-verifying signal: if a candidate range decompresses and its checksum matches, that range is almost certainly a real stored file chunk. Scanning for these ranges produced 2,241,410 streams across the corpus, every one checksum-verified.

From there the reasoning chain is:

flowchart TD
    S["Scan for zlib headers"] --> V["Decompress + checksum"]
    V --> R["Verified byte ranges"]
    R --> C["Group into chains<br/>(64 KiB continuations)"]
    R --> E["Group into entries<br/>(struct + data, or chains)"]
    C --> N["Compare with declared counts"]
    E --> N
    N --> X["Exact entry boundaries<br/>without reading the table"]

The scan tells us where the bytes are. It does not tell us which file is which, or what the file means. Those are separate problems, solved separately.

docs.title: 3. What the unreadable metadata still tells us
docs.text:
Even unreadable bytes leak sizes. Three size laws fell out of a census of 4,373 headers:

  • the trailer length is stored in the header and always matches the trailing region (+0x0c);
  • Front B — the entry table — is exactly align16(stride · N) where N is the declared entry count, for all 2,908 headers of the dominant mode family;
  • the stride is 9 bytes for one format tag and 10 for another, and the tag is chosen by the count itself (small packs vs large packs).

The table's contents are unreadable, but its shape is known, and — crucially — so is how many entries each pack declares. That number becomes the yard stick for the payload work: if a payload reconstruction produces exactly N entries, the reconstruction is very likely right.

This is the key methodological move of the project:

Use the unreadable table as an oracle for counting, and the payload for structure.

docs.title: 4. Reconstructing entries from the payload
docs.text:
Payloads come in two self-describing shapes, and each archive uses one:

Pairs. A small stream — a struct — immediately followed by its data stream. The struct is a little record of fields: tagged pointers, an orientation basis, two identifiers, and the exact size of the data that follows. In core_bvh4 the struct is 208 bytes and this pairing holds for 3,967 of 4,000 sampled entries.

Chains. A large file is stored as 64 KiB chunks; a chunk continues its predecessor when the predecessor decoded exactly 65,536 bytes and the next stream starts on the 16-byte boundary after it. One chain = one entry. data and navmeshes use this shape.

flowchart LR
    subgraph pair["Pair shape"]
      D["struct<br/>208 B"] --> F["data stream<br/>exact size at +0xa0"]
    end
    subgraph chain["Chain shape"]
      C1["chunk 64 KiB"] --> C2["chunk 64 KiB"] --> C3["final chunk"]
    end

Because the struct declares the data size, the pair shape is exact: the descriptor predicts a byte range, the range decompresses, and every byte past the declared size is zero (verified on re-decoded samples). That is the project's first milestone: one decoded record independently predicts a checksum-verified byte range.

docs.title: 5. From numbers to names
docs.text:
Every identifier in the object graph, bone tables and weight arrays is JOAAT, the one-at-a-time hash: a specific 32-bit function of a string.

That scope matters. Archive entry names are not JOAAT: the executable hashes them with Murmur3 x64-128 over tolower(name) with \\ folded to /, and then resolves them through a 16-bit id taken from a runtime dictionary (the executable). So JOAAT is the hash of content names, not of file names.

That turns "opaque number" into "guess the string, test the hash". With a vocabulary of rig concepts resolved 99 of 612 bone-table hashes and 21 of 252 weight hashes. The names came out in three families:

Prefix Meaning Example skel_ skeleton bone skel_l_calf mh_ muscle helper mh_l_bicep rb_ ragdoll body rb_l_shoulder01

One rig is now fully decoded: 34 bones, symmetric left/right blocks with a constant index offset — a hand/forearm rig with four three-segment finger chains.

docs.title: 6. The media layer
docs.text:
Some payloads are not game data at all. The large "unclassified" spans turned out to be media containers:

Container Signature Content AWC ADAT game audio (Opus, XMA2, ACE1 impulse responses) Bink / Bink2 BIK, KB2n video

Two AWC layout families were decoded and one of them, in story000, produced 196,350 Opus streams / 148.3 hours of audio. That is why the "unknown bytes" figure collapsed from 52.8 GB to essentially zero: it was audio and video, not unnamed assets.

docs.title: 8. What is still open, and why
docs.text:
Not everything is solved. The honest boundary:

  • Metadata record contents. The loader copies both metadata buffers verbatim and the layout is code-derived, so the container is understood — but what the records mean is not. No 32-bit or 64-bit hash of any known name appears in them, and the archive's own name hash is Murmur3 x64-128 whose 16-bit id comes from a runtime dictionary whose source has not been located. Naming those records is the open problem, and it is information-blocked, not effort-blocked.
  • Names. 330 bone hashes belong to a namespace whose vocabulary has not been found — small props and weapons, not anatomy.
  • Mixed packs. Packs whose entries mix both shapes cannot be counted exactly; the manifests mark them rather than guessing.

Everything else in this site is built on the chain above: checksums give ranges, sizes give counts, structures give entries, hashes give names.

docs.title: Findings
docs.text: A summary of the verified results, written for a reader who has not followed the journal. Each claim links to the page or artifact that proves it; the append-only evidence lives in investigation.md.

docs.title: The container
docs.text:
RPF9 is a 0x60-byte header followed by three metadata regions and a payload:

Region Bounds State Header 0x00..0x60 mapped, 24 words Buffer A 0x00..+0x04 read verbatim; 0x40-byte header + four sections + one record per entry Buffer B +0x08..+0x04 read verbatim; fixed-stride per-entry table (align16(N × stride)) Payload Front B end .. trailer zlib chains, opaque spans, zero runs Trailer end - +0x0c .. end content unidentified; pack-independent length

The header fields are known well enough to predict sizes without decoding: +0x0c is the trailer length in all 4,373 headers censused, and Front B is align16(9N) or align16(10N) exactly — selected by a count-driven tag — for all 2,908 mode-family-1 headers. Every payload stream is located by scanning and checksum verification, not by the table.

docs.title: Coverage
docs.text:
All 22 source archives are indexed: 4,415,868 ranges / 161.3 GB stored / 365.0 GB decoded, and every index tiles its archive exactly, with no gap and no overlap. Six archives plus levels carry bulk extraction manifests covering 2,190,635 zlib ranges; each extraction is SHA-256 verified.

The unclassified layer is closed: every large span is media. 38.1 GB of AWC audio, 13.4 GB of Bink/Bink2 video, ~1.2 GB of fragments. There is no unexplained game payload left in it.

docs.title: Entry identity from the payload
docs.text:
The index table's records are unidentified, so entries are identified from the payload instead:

Archive Unit Packs verified Entries core_bvh4 pairs 1,253 / 1,261 109,301 navmeshes chains 14 / 28 23,530 packs pairs 20 / 59 15,983 levels pairs 728 / 2,044 29,117 anim chains 125 / 235 5,826 data chains 16 / 40 2,063 textures pairs 17 / 20 1,326

188,298 entries with exact, payload-derived boundaries and an independent check against the declared count, across 14 archives; the table above shows the largest. Every pack contributed only when its entry count verified exactly, and the full per-archive table is the corpus pass.

docs.title: Naming
docs.text:
Archive entry names are a different function: Murmur3 x64-128 with a lower-casing substitution table, resolved to a 16-bit id from a runtime dictionary (the executable). JOAAT below refers to content names.

Every identifier encountered in the object graph, bones and weight arrays is JOAAT(lowercase name). That single fact turned hash tables into readable rigs:

  • 99 of 612 class-0 bone-table hashes and 21 of 252 weight hashes resolve through the skel_ / mh_ / rb_ families (skeleton, muscle helpers, ragdoll).
  • One rig is fully decoded: root 0x48dcbb01, 34/34 bones — a two-sided hand/forearm rig with four three-segment finger chains.
  • The 16 skeleton families carry readings: a hand rig, a genital rig, large animals, and a small-prop population that still holds an unnamed 330-hash universe.

docs.title: Audio
docs.text:
audio.rpf's 23.5 GB of AWC containers decode completely: 93,344 Opus, 1,818 XMA2 and 73 ACE1 streams with zero failures. The check that makes it trustworthy is frames × channels / declared, which is 1.002 at the 1st percentile — the declared count is interleaved across channels, so a naive frames / declared halves every stereo stream.

story000 turned out to hold a second, larger audio archive: 9.56 GB of AWC in a different container variant, decoded to 196,350 Opus streams / 148.3 hours.

The three container variants share one record format (type:8 | size:28 | offset:28) but not one table position. 0xff02 computes it; 0xff21/0xff61 carry it as the longest valid 8-byte-aligned suffix before the data offset, which a scan finds every time (tools/awc_chunk_table.py).

docs.title: Script schema
docs.text:
script.rpf records are a chunk chain, not bytecode, and the chain was recovered from the writer in the executable rather than inferred. PSIN holds a flat array of 16-byte rows (property, key, value, type): 63,288 rows across 1,012 records, of which 42 % now name their property (164 distinct properties, 14,530 distinct keys). The type word is the last field of the row; an earlier extractor was misaligned by 8 bytes and paired every value with the next row's property, which is why coverage looked like 4 % before.

PSIN itself is a general envelope — ≈18,637 records across ten archives — but the property array is a single-file feature: scanning every body at every byte offset finds rows only in script.rpf (plus 28 rows in two packs.rpf records). Three layouts carry the envelope, and the other two hold different payloads.

The same container appears in levels.rpf, where streams carry the identical section sequence but a different payload: a bag of tagged sections rather than one typed table. Over the first 400 records there are 209 distinct section tags and the descriptor count varies from 2 to 17+, because a level only carries the sections it needs. Two of those sections hold NUL-padded ASCII resource paths — 3,697 distinct paths harvested from 6,982 records, e.g. acaidreams_protectedarea/all.pso.meta.

LSNS is a table container, not a cipher: framing validates on 1,012 of 1,012 records, 58,697 sixteen-byte records. Each table is [path of ≤10 × 128-bit levels][per-script tail], and the path is a trie — 853 tables share level 1, 381 share all ten — so it encodes a hierarchy of script kinds while its labels stay opaque.

docs.title: What is not solved
docs.text:
• The metadata record contents are unidentified. The loader copies both buffers verbatim, so a transform would have to live in the stream's Read; the sizes are known and the contents are not. That is measured rather than assumed: 36,952 known names hashed with seven functions in twenty path normalizations produce a flat ~560 matches per function against 7.4 million front-region words, which is exactly the chance rate — no hash function, including the game's own joaat, shows any excess. The read→mount→entry-walk path contains no cipher call. Four metadata questions are blocked on key material or a crib, not on effort.
  • The remaining 330-hash universe is a vocabulary problem: the names are not in the corpora harvested so far.
  • core_bvh4 reproduces the declared count for 1,253 of 1,261 packs; the rest, and most of levels, have one to four entries per pack whose descriptor is not where the stream window says it should be.

See plan.md for the live list.

    autonumber
    participant U as User
    participant CLI as rage-tools-vi
    participant Z as flate2

        CLI->>Z: decode checksum-valid zlib

Design boundary

extract-zlib validates framing and checksums. It deliberately does not interpret PSIN, LSCH, LSNS, or any object record.

docs.title: Script schema (PSIN)
docs.text:
script.rpf records are not bytecode. Each record is a chain of chunks, and the script schema lives inside them.

The format below is not inferred from the corpus. It was read out of the writer in the executable — FUN_144083410 — found by scanning .text for the chunk magics, each of which occurs exactly once and all inside that one function. When the recovered layout and the bytes disagree, the bytes win, and the checks below are exact rather than statistical.

docs.title: The chunk chain
docs.text:
Every chunk is [4-byte ASCII magic][big-endian u32: distance to the next chunk]. Nothing else is stored: no sizes, no counts, no terminator.

PSIN → LSCH → LENM → LSNS → LGID → LRSC

Every record ends with a seventh chunk, CHKS. The order is fixed.

Two traps cost us real time and are worth naming:

  • The header word is big-endian while the payload words are little-endian. That is why an old helper that read a big-endian size happened to work: the "size" it read is the distance to the next chunk.
  • 0x4d4e454c is LENM, not LMEN. A scan for the wrong spelling reports zero occurrences and looks like evidence that the chunk does not exist.

docs.title: Anatomy of one record
docs.text:
Record 42 of script.rpf, 5,392 bytes after decompression — the whole chain, with each chunk's distance and payload size:

0x0000  PSIN  distance 0x0d60  payload 3,416 B  count 4 sections
0x0d60  LSCH  distance 0x01d8  payload   464 B  count 3 index rows
0x0f38  LENM  distance 0x0080  payload   120 B  count 1 index row
0x0fb8  LSNS  distance 0x04e4  payload 1,244 B  opaque table block
0x149c  LGID  distance 0x0008  payload     0 B  empty list
0x14a4  LRSC  distance 0x0058  payload    80 B  fixed header block
0x14fc  CHKS  distance 0x0014  payload    12 B  size + tag
0x1510  end of body

0x14fc + 0x14 = 0x1510 — the chain ends on the last byte. Reproduce with:

uv run python tools/script_meta.py --index output/index/script.tsv --dump 1

docs.title: PSIN: the section table
docs.text:
+0x00  'PSIN'
+0x04  u32 BE  distance to LSCH
+0x08  count × 16-byte descriptors
          +0x00  u32  section tag
          +0x04  u32  payload length
          +0x08  u64  0xAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAA   (pointer, poisoned on disk)
       then each descriptor's payload, in order, each rounded up to 16 bytes

count is not stored. It is recovered by asking which value closes the arithmetic exactly:

16*count + 0x10 + Σ align16(length_i)  ==  distance_to_next_chunk

The first payload starts at 16*count + 0x10 because the writer computes (16*count + 0x17) & ~15, which rounds down. Using an ordinary round-up alignment helper puts every payload 16 bytes late.

The 0xAA runs that earlier scans treated as a terminator are these poisoned pointers — the same trick appears as 0xEE in LENM and 0xBB in LRSC.

docs.title: The typed block
docs.text:
In script.rpf the sections are almost constant, five tags per record:

tag role records 0x85b4c631 typed rows 1,012 0xde396fe2 80-byte sub-table directory 1,012 0x01393259 struct-like block 1,012 0x16 16-byte rows, 128-bit material 1,010 0xaeb623d8 12-byte {u32, f32, f32} triples 855

The typed rows are 16 bytes each and the type word sits at the end:

struct PsinRow {          // 63,288 rows across 1,012 records
    u32 property;         // 164 distinct — Flags, Heading, Position, Name, Id, ...
    u32 key;              // 14,530 distinct — the object keys
    u32 value;            // value or reference, see the open question below
    u32 type;             // 0x101 int, 0x102 float, 0x103 hash, 0x104 bool, 0x105 byte
};

Type distribution across the corpus: byte 20,005 · float 15,277 · hash 14,739 · int 13,257 · bool 10.

docs.title: Correction: an earlier extraction was shifted by 8 bytes
docs.text:
The first extractor sliced each record at offset + 8, which put its 16-byte grid 8 bytes early. Its type column was therefore the real +0x0c word — correct by accident — but its property and key columns came from the next physical row. Values were being paired with the following row's property.

Fixing the alignment changed what the data looks like: property coverage went from 4.3 % of rows named to 42 % (26,893 of 63,288), and the dominant entry pair became Heading + Position (2,807 pairs), which is what a flattened placement schema should look like.

docs.title: LSCH: the index over sections
docs.text:
LSCH rows are 32 bytes and name the sections:

+0x00  u32  section tag          <- one of this record's PSIN tags (200/200 records)
+0x04  u32  hash
+0x08  u32  small value
+0x0c  u32  zero
+0x10  u64  pointer              <- poisoned 0xAA on disk
+0x18  u32  value
+0x1c  u16  zero
+0x1e  u16  sub-record count
       then sub-records, 16 bytes each, appended after the rows

Sub-records carry a tag at +0x0c, so the record cross-references itself twice. LENM rows have the same shape in 24 bytes (tag, hash, poisoned pointer, u16 sub-count at +0x10).

None of the index fields is a count of its section: tested against both the block byte length and the row count over 4,901 sections, the best agreement is 36.7 %, which is a computed length rather than the literal size. The exact-fit solve stays the only count oracle.

docs.title: levels records look different
docs.text: Same chain, different content: a levels PSIN is a bag of tagged sections. Over the first 400 records there are 209 distinct tags, and the descriptor count varies from 2 to 17+ depending on what the level contains. 0x78ba5fa7 and 0xec610df1 carry NUL-padded ASCII resource paths, for example acaidreams_protectedarea/all.pso.meta — 3,697 distinct paths across 6,982 records.

docs.title: CHKS
docs.text: Twelve bytes: a big-endian total record size (matches the decompressed body length in 60/60 records) followed by a 4-byte tag not yet identified. Candidates joaat32, fnv1a, crc32 and adler32 over the body, the body prefix and the compressed stream are all excluded.

docs.text: handoff/psin-rows.tsv (63,288 rows) and handoff/script-sections.tsv (4,901 sections) are generated — by tools/psin_blocks.py --rows and tools/script_sections.py respectively. handoff/psin-vocabulary.tsv is curated by hand: it lists named PSIN values grouped by a lower-cased English property name (flag, name, weapon_group, vehicle_class), and no rule tried so far reproduces it from the rows alone. Treat it as a vocabulary table, not as output, and do not overwrite it from a script.

docs.title: Running the parser
docs.text:
# whole corpus, chain census and a decoded sample
uv run python tools/script_meta.py script.rpf --index output/index/script.tsv --dump 1

# the five sections side by side, corrected field order
uv run python tools/psin_blocks.py --index output/index/script.tsv --show 1

# joined PSIN + LSCH view
uv run python tools/script_sections.py --out handoff/script-sections.tsv

# levels section census and path harvest
uv run python tools/levels_sections.py --archive "$SRC/levels.rpf" \
    --index output/index/levels.tsv --limit 400
uv run python tools/levels_paths.py --archive "$SRC/levels.rpf" \
    --index output/index/levels.tsv

Validation: 1,012 / 1,012 records produce the complete seven-chunk chain, and the chain covers each decompressed body exactly — the last chunk's distance ends on the final byte, with zero slack. That is the check that would have caught an unlisted magic: a missing chunk type would leave the body longer than the chain. It is enforced by tools/script_meta.py --verify, and the earlier six-chunk reading in an earlier reading fell into exactly that trap, and the typed-word count agrees with the olderer independent heuristic scan to 0.6 % (63,290 vs 62,910).

docs.title: Textures
docs.text: Texture dictionaries are descriptor-backed. Their bounds, names, and dimensions validate. The single-mip controls verify BC3 for 0x4d and BC7 for 0x62.

The validated relation is:

stored_bytes = blocks × stride

Dimensions, format code, hash, pointer, stride, and bounds agree. That is not a pixel decode.

docs.title: Verified controls
docs.text:
The 64×64 trophy texture in textures.rpf fills a single 4 KiB buffer with 256 BC3 blocks starting at offset zero. All block addresses match the low 4 KiB of the 2D 128-bpp standard swizzle. The decoded PNG and reproduction command are listed in handoff/texture-trophy-control.md.

The 172×172 switch_jason control uses a row-major 3×3 grid of 4 KiB pages. Each page uses the same within-page pattern. All 1,849 active blocks have valid BC7 modes, and all 455 omitted blocks are zero padding. The page-row stride is 0x3000 bytes and cropped linear pitch is 688 bytes. See handoff/texture-bc7-control.md for the address formula and PNG.

docs.title: Audio (audio.rpf)
docs.text: audio.rpf contains 6,625 ADAT AWC containers / 23.51 GB. The GTA VI container is a new layout, not the GTA V AWC format parsed by vgmstream.

docs.title: Container variants
docs.text:
Three flag families are known, and the payload layout differs between them:

Flags data_offset Per-stream header Chunk table Status 0xff21 20 + 42·n 42 B at 0x50, 8-byte records decoded 0xff02 16 + 60·n 60 B at 0x10 + 4·n decoded 0xff25 compact — ends at data_offset open 0xff61 — — — decoded (rare)

A chunk record is a little-endian u64 packing offset:28 | size:28 | type:8, so the type byte is the record's high byte. 0xff02 streams own exactly seven chunks, in order 0x36 0x55 0x5c 0x76 0xa3 0xb2 0xbd.

Field 0xff21 0xff02 stream index at +0x10 u16[n], monotonic none; 4·n bytes of per-stream data data_offset (6 streams) 0x110 0x82 0x76 rate low u16 at +0x08 (0xBB80 = 48 kHz) same

The 0x76 descriptor is 32 bytes: sample count at +0x00/+0x0c, rate as the low u16 at +0x08, codec at +0x1c, codec sub-ID at +0x1d. Reading the rate as a u32 yields nonsense on both variants.

docs.title: The per-stream word
docs.text:
The field that decides how many chunks a stream owns is a single u32, and its two halves do different jobs:

 31              3 2   0
+-----------------+-----+
|   stream id     | tags|
+-----------------+-----+
  29 bits           3 bits

The tag count sits in the high three bits, not the low ones. Reading it as a plain integer gives a stream id in the millions for ordinary streams, which is what made the first parser look broken; masking the top three bits yields sensible ids, and masking the bottom three yields chunk counts that match the chunk table exactly.

This is also why the chunk-table search had to be a suffix scan: the table is located relative to data_offset, and data_offset depends on the tag count, so the two have to be solved together (tools/awc_chunk_table.py).

Verification state

The bit split above is stated in the upstream layout notes and is consistent with every stream decoded so far (93,344 Opus, 1,818 XMA2, 73 ACE1, zero failures), but it has not been re-derived as a standalone measurement since the extraction volume went offline. Treat it as inherited-but-consistent rather than freshly counted.

docs.title: story000 cutscene audio
docs.text:
story000's 9.56 GB unclassified span is a second audio archive: 63,853 AWC containers, 98.4 % 0xff02, all codec 0x0b (Opus) at 48 kHz. A whole-file scan with the rules above indexes 63,325 banks / 9,212,590,080 B = 46.011 % of that 20 GB archive, and raises its classified share from 35.39 % to 81.40 % (output/index/story000-adat.tsv). Decoding it produced 196,350 streams / 148.3 hours / 47.7 GB of WAV in output/extracted/story000-opus/. Opus packets are framed [u16 size][packet] inside 0x800-byte blocks, the same as audio.rpf.

Tools: tools/awc_framing_ff02.py (variant census) and tools/extract_awc_ff02.py (WAV export with manifest and SHA-256).

The 0x76 descriptor is 32 bytes: sample count at +0x00/+0x0c, sample rate at +0x08, codec at +0x1c, and codec sub-ID at +0x1d.

docs.title: Index coverage
docs.text:
The original stream index classified 99.93 % of audio.rpf as unclassified — it recognises compressions, and an AWC bank is neither compressed nor opaque. That was an index gap, not missing data, and it is now closed:

source banks bytes extraction manifest (0xff21 pass) 6,625 23,510,392,992 gaps between them (0xff21, 0xff02, 0xff61) 534 4,943,599,616 total 7,159 28,453,992,608 = 99.687 %

Both variants share one rule: the chunk table holds four records per stream and ends exactly at header_size, with type:8 | size:28 | offset:28 per record. Only the table's start differs — 0x50 for 0xff21, 0x10 + 4·count for 0xff02. A bank ends where its furthest record ends, rounded up to 0x800.

Three rules finish the job, applied in this order:

  1. a computable table position (0xff21 at 0x50, 0xff02 at 0x10 + 4·count), with records-per-stream derived from header_size rather than assumed;
  2. a suffix scan — the longest valid 8-byte record run ending at header_size — for 0xff25/0xff61, which carry no computable position;
  3. the same suffix scan as a fallback when the computable rule does not close, which catches banks carrying an extra per-stream table (one bank needed exactly this).

Scan alignment is 4 bytes, not 0x800: most banks are 0x800-aligned but a handful sit on a 4-byte boundary. Validation is what keeps the looser scan honest.

The residual 0.313 % (89,462,064 B, 275 gaps) is accounted for: 19,509,248 B is the archive's own front region, and the other 69,952,816 B are regions where ADAT bytes exist but no candidate validates at any offset shift — the bytes are not a container header there.

A magic scan alone does not validate: ADAT occurs at 7,159 aligned offsets in audio.rpf, and none validate against awc_parse.py's tag model, because that model is the Leonida/story000 layout rather than the 0xff21/0xff02 one. Validating one layout with the other yields confident garbage — which is exactly what the first 7,159 rejections were.

docs.title: How much audio there is
docs.text:
Reading each container's chunk table, without decoding anything (tools/extract_adat_gaps.py + tools/audio_census_totals.py):

archive containers streams stream data audio.rpf 7,159 1,606,237 22.47 GB story000.rpf 63,325 213,579 6.06 GB total 70,484 1,819,816 28.53 GB codec in the corpus decoded share opus 1,795,416 93,344 5.2 % xma2 1,818 1,818 100 % ace1 227 73 32 %

The XMA2 number is the control: 1,818 obtained by decoding and 1,818 from the chunk tables, by independent paths. So the tables are read correctly, and the Opus figure means the decode passes covered about a twentieth of the streams that exist.

Container flags in audio.rpf: 0xff25 3,008, 0xff02 2,071, 0xff21 1,270 — the compact variant dominates, which is why the first extraction pass (a 0xff21 scan) under-counted the archive so badly.

docs.title: Decoding a previously missed container
docs.text:
The old probe looked for the data offset at +0x0c — the 0xff21 layout — so it found nothing in the 0xff02 pools. tools/decode_adat_stream.py uses the verified table rules instead, and the first stream from an untouched container decodes:

audio.rpf+0x16437000  (0xff02, 1,914 streams)
stream 0: Opus, mono, declared 32,000 Hz, 116,480 samples
          4,096 B payload -> 124 packets -> 119,040 samples = 2.48 s
          peak 0.743 FS, RMS 0.107 FS — not silence

Two details worth knowing before decoding at scale:

  • the 0x76 rate is the source rate (32 kHz here, 48 kHz in the packs measured earlier); libopus only produces 48 kHz and rejects other rates with OPUS_BAD_ARG, so always decode at 48 kHz;
  • the decoded length is ~2 % longer than the declared sample count, because the declared value is post-trim.

docs.title: Decode coverage by variant
docs.text:
A sample of 24 evenly spaced containers, 8 streams each (tools/decode_adat_sample.py):

variant containers streams decoded audio 0xff02 9 72 3.0 min 0xff21 5 32 2.7 min 0xff61 1 8 0.1 min 0xff25 9 0 —

112 streams, 5.8 minutes, median RMS 0.13 FS, 2 near-silent. 0xff61 decodes once its table is found by suffix scan.

0xff25 has no chunk table at all. A sampled container reports count = 2, header_size = 64, and inside the header there is an inline descriptor ending 07 00 | 80 bb | 0b | 01 | ff ff — flags, 0xbb80 (48 000 Hz), codec, channels, terminator. Over 600 such containers, 95.3 % are Opus (codec 0x0b) at 48 kHz with one or two channels; stereo is the majority (401 stereo, 171 mono).

So the compact variant describes its streams in place rather than through records, which is why the table model found nothing.

Two further probes narrowed it without solving it: only 32 of 200 containers admit a valid 8-byte table under any byte shift (two records per stream where they do), and no field in the first 64 bytes scales with the container size. The type-like bytes sit at odd offsets (0x23, 0x2b, 0x2f, 0x3f), so the alignment is not the one the other variants use.

Further tests, all negative except one identification: no block framing at sizes 0x100–0x2000 and shifts 0–3; packet chains stop after 12–25 packets; and the repeated payload offset +0x860 holds the a0 00 f8 marker already documented in tools/awc_framing.py, not packet data. Big-endian u16 and little-endian u32 length prefixes both fail there too.

Decodable, with a common framing. Many 0xff25 containers are a sequence of 0x800-byte blocks carrying packets from block + 0x60; measured over 300 sampled containers that holds for 42 % of those that parse (first offset) and 58 % (period), and 45 % produce no 8-packet run under it at all. So it is a fast path, not a definition. Decoding packet by packet gives, from one 266 KB container:

3,049 packets -> 60.98 s stereo   RMS 0.176   spectral flatness 0.0045

The variant that contributed nothing to every earlier pass accounts for 100.96 hours of audio across its 3,008 containers (3,008 decoded, 65.0 GiB WAV) in audio.rpf. Decode with tools/decode_adat_stream.py --ff25.

Earlier measurements that bounded the problem, retained because they explain why the structural routes failed:

  • the body entropy is 7.74–7.79 against 3.4–4.4 for the header, so the containers do hold audio;
  • header_size is not the data start — one container with header_size = 64 has the … 80 bb 0b 01 ff ff descriptor sitting at offset 64, so the descriptor block extends past it;
  • the payload is packet-framed but not block-framed: scanning a whole container finds 1,678 short runs of ≥12 valid size-prefixed packets, while all 130 0x800-aligned blocks fail the other variants' block rule;
  • a table-like run in the header is an arithmetic sequence of step 90 read one byte in, the third independent sign that this variant's fields sit at odd offsets.

What is not yet located is the payload start and the split between streams; until both exist, no 0xff25 stream is decoded, and the census keeps its 3,008 containers' streams out of the decoded totals.

docs.title: Codec status
docs.text:
The corpus scan found 2,320 parsed streams:

Codec Streams Status 0x0b 2,081 Opus; decoded 0x05 166 XMA2; decoded 0x02 73 ACE1 impulse responses; decoded

docs.title: 0x05 = XMA2
docs.text: The first wrapper used wFormatTag=0x0161 (WMAudio2), so ffmpeg called the wrong decoder. The correct XMA2 tag is 0x0166. With it, 151 unique streams decode to 86 MB of PCM WAV; all 151 are non-silent and 148 have spectral flatness below 0.1. The engine rumble in the decoded set is a human-confirmed check. The 15 missing 0x05 rows are fragmented AWC entries.

docs.title: 0x0B = Opus
docs.text:
Each 0x800-byte 0x55 block is a sequence of

[u16le packet size][size-byte Opus packet] ...
zero padding to the block end

The a0 00 f8 prefix is a 160-byte packet (f8 is its TOC); the next packet starts at 162. libopus decodes the controls at 48 kHz, and every 0xA3 block boundary matches cumulative decoded frames × channels.

Bulk export: 2,081/2,081 streams / 2.5 GB untrimmed WAV, zero decode failures. 11 non-48 kHz streams are decoded at 48 kHz with source rate recorded; 5 seek flags and 1 encoded silence are preserved. Pre-skip and end-trim are bounded by controls but not exactly determined.

docs.title: 0x02 = ACE1 impulse responses
docs.text:
Each 0x2000-byte tile is 1,024 interleaved complex float32 bins of a 2,048-point real FFT, stored with the Nyquist bin omitted. Inverse-transform the tiles, restore the missing alternating Nyquist component from the zero leading half and adjacent overlaps, concatenate the second halves, and trim to the tap count at 0x76 +0x0c. The terminal 0x2000 bytes are an ACE1 trailer: 0xfffface1 + 15 LE u16 pairs + zero padding.

tools/extract_awc_ace1.py exported 73/73 streams / 6 MB float32 WAV; all controls have overlap/padding RMS below 8e-9. The first trailer pair values are not needed for reconstruction and remain unassigned.

docs.title: BVH4 entries (core_bvh4)
docs.text:
core_bvh4.rpf stores its entries as a contiguous pair of zlib streams: a 208-byte descriptor followed by one data stream. Over a 4,000-entry sample the stream after a descriptor is that entry's data and the stream after the data is the next descriptor in 3,967 / 4,000 cases.

This makes core_bvh4 the first archive where entry boundaries are recoverable from the payload alone. The generated manifest handoff/core-bvh4-entries.tsv lists 296,490 entries over 1,282 packs:

Shape Entries pair (descriptor + data) 269,106 struct (small struct, plus any following > 64 KiB streams) 25,507 orphan 1

1,253 of 1,261 packs have an entry count exactly equal to their declared N. The residual is ±1 in 41 packs, ±2–5 in 12, and one outlier: the root pack, whose 1,286 "entries" are the nested packs rather than streams — an independent confirmation that a pack's declared count includes its child packs.

docs.title: Descriptor (208 bytes, 13 × 16)
docs.text:
Offsets Content Evidence +0x00..+0x3F constant template: eight u32 slots, six of them 0x5/0x6-tagged self-relative pointers offsets land inside the record; the 256-byte header-only variant uses 0xb0…0xf0 +0x40, +0x44 two per-entry 32-bit ids 3,811 distinct of 4,000 +0x50..+0x7F right-handed orthonormal 3×3 basis, rows at +0x50, +0x60, +0x70, each padded to 16 bytes orthonormal 4,000/4,000, det > 0, worst error 4.2e-05 +0x80, +0x84 zero constant +0x88 0x00000101 constant +0x90..+0x9F zero constant +0xa0 allocated payload size, multiple of 256 zero-padded tail verified on 260 samples +0xa4 two u16: low multiple of 64, high multiple of 256 both bounded by the allocated size; (lo - 0x100) % 64 == 0; reads as offsets, role open +0xa8..+0xCF zero constant 
classDiagram
    class Descriptor {
        +template: 0x40 bytes
        +id0: u32
        +id1: u32
        +basis: 3 x vec3 (row padded)
        +flags: u32 = 0x101
        +allocated: u32
        +pair: u16lo x u16hi
    }
    class Payload {
        +header: 0x100 bytes
        +used: u64 at +0x20
        +used_minus_256: u64 at +0x28

        +tail_count: u32 at used-4
    }
    Descriptor "1" --> "1" Payload : next stream

docs.title: The template is a struct, not a record type
docs.text:
The same template appears in descriptor-less entries, which are the small header-only streams found where a pack's descriptor count falls short of its declared N (27,373 streams, median 272 bytes). Their +0x00..+0x3F slots hold the same eight values, but the tagged pointers move to 0xb0, 0xd0, 0xe0, 0xf0 and the +0x10 count becomes 2. So the 208-byte descriptor and those 256-byte records are the same serialized struct at different sizes, with self-relative 0x5-tagged pointers and one 0x6-tagged field. Within a size class the header is byte-identical.

The struct is an {ptr, u16 count, u16 capacity} container family: the pairs 0x00010001 (1/1) in the 160-byte record and 0x00040004 (4/4) in the 272-byte record are count/capacity. The 272-byte record holds an array of four element pointers at 0xc0, each element a 32-byte record with an 8-byte hash at +0x10.

docs.title: Payload
docs.text:
• +0x00..+0x1F and +0x30..+0xFF are zero; the body starts at +0x100.
  • +0x20 is the used size: it equals last_non_zero_byte + 3 in 160/160 sampled payloads and is always a multiple of 4.
  • +0x28 = +0x20 − 256 in 160/160.
  • The descriptor's +0xa0 is the used size rounded up to a multiple of 64 (gaps 0, 64, 128, 192), and a multiple of 256.
  • The last four bytes before the used end are a small little-endian u32 (1…15 observed, all ≤ 255), followed by three zero bytes. It grows monotonically with payload size and is count-like; a log2 size class is falsified (48 %).
  • Body data is sparse (~8 % non-zero), with 64-byte records, 0x81-filled regions of exactly 2,048 bytes (32 nodes) at 64-byte boundaries, and a value table packed at a 3-byte stride.

docs.title: What is ruled out
docs.text:
• 0x81 is not a fixed-lane -127 sentinel: it occupies every offset of the 64-byte frame about equally (5,760–5,955 per offset, 25 % below offset 16, the uniform share). It does appear as whole-node fills at 64-byte boundaries.
  • The two ids are not JOAAT/CRC32 of the 3,524-name bone corpus or 1,087 local path tokens, not CRC32/JOAAT of the payload or stored bytes, and do not appear inside the payload.
  • +0xa4 is not a span pair (hi < lo in 3 of 16, and (used - hi) % 3 is uniform so it is not the tail index table) and not a node count (lo/64 = 144 against 16,273 non-zero 64-byte records in one sample). It is bounded like an offset pair: lo and hi are both ≤ the allocated size, and in the decoded 768-byte entry lo is exactly 0x100 (body start) and hi exactly 0x200.

docs.title: Entry manifests
docs.text: The RPF9 index records are unidentified, so entries are identified from the payload instead: a pack's streams pair into entries, and the declared count N is used as an independent check rather than as the parser's driver. The loader copies the metadata buffers verbatim, so a transform — if one exists — would sit in the stream's Read, not in the archive layer.

docs.title: Units
docs.text:
Two payload shapes appear, and each archive uses whichever one its entries have:

  • pair — a struct stream followed by its data stream. Used by core_bvh4 (208-byte descriptor) and textures (256–1,184-byte structs).
  • chain — a 64 KiB chain group, where a stream continues its predecessor if the predecessor decoded exactly 65,536 bytes and this stream starts on the align16 boundary of its end. Used by data and navmeshes.

An entry is emitted only when the pack's item count lands within a small tolerance of N; each row carries the delta and a declared_ok style flag, so a consumer can filter to exact packs.

docs.title: Verification
docs.text:
Each manifest is checked against its archive index:

  • every entry's stream and data offsets exist in the zlib index — 0 missing;
  • no stream appears twice inside a pack — 0 duplicates;
  • entry counts sit within the emit tolerance of N.

The core_bvh4 residual (20 packs beyond tolerance) is the known family whose declared N counts child packs or mixed entry shapes; those rows are emitted with declared_ok = 0.

docs.title: Why this works without the table
docs.text:
The payload structures are self-describing:

  • core_bvh4's descriptor carries the entry's exact payload size at +0xa0 (zero-padding verified beyond it), a right-handed orthonormal basis (269,105 / 269,106 within 1e-3), and two content ids whose duplicates always share one allocated size.
  • textures and navmeshes structs open with tagged self-relative pointers; navmeshes points outside its own stream, which is why the classifier accepts alignment alone as the pointer filter.
  • Chain grouping needs no decode at all, so data and navmeshes manifests are reproducible from the index alone.

docs.title: Serialized structs across the corpus
docs.text:
Most entry payloads open with a serialized container struct: eight 4-byte slots whose values are 0x5-tagged self-relative pointers (0x50000080 = tag 5, offset 0x80), one 0x6-tagged field, and {ptr, u16 count, u16 capacity} array headers. The scanner identifies a struct when the first 0x40 bytes (at offset 0, or after a 256-byte payload header) hold at least two such pointers, where a candidate is a u32 with upper nibble 5..0xA and low four bits zero.

Guardrails learned the hard way:

  • scan the header only; whole-payload scanning invents dozens of pointers per 6 MB body;
  • +0xa0 is a bvh4 class field, not a container field — it is harvested only when the record is 208 bytes and carries the full bvh4 pointer table (0x50000080/a0/b0/c0/50, 1 at +0x10, 0x60000000 at +0x20);
  • tag-5 targets need not stay inside the stream. core_bvh4's descriptor points inside its own 208 bytes, but navmeshes structs point far outside (a 1,840-byte body holds 0x53149a19, target 0x3149a19). Requiring an in-body target rejected 2,446 of 2,447 navmeshes structs; alignment alone is the correct filter, and the shares in the table below are therefore lower bounds for archives whose pointers leave their stream.

docs.title: The executable as a source
docs.text:
Every claim about a format here is one of three kinds: inferred from the corpus, measured against the corpus, or read out of the executable. This page is the third kind — the functions, where they live, and exactly what each one settles.

Where the bytes and the code disagreed, the code won: it corrected the script row field order, the chunk count, and the buffer-B relationship.

docs.title: The binary
docs.text:
Field Value file game_scarlett_master.exe size 120,181,760 B sha256 e95020b2fa4a721db3df59fdecf75621730ac559d8835252f6c3b658d5a08993 format PE32+ x86-64, 10 sections, image base 0x140000000 build timestamp 1794606036 → 2026-11-13 provenance .xbld, .retplne, .voltbl sections; imports d3d12_xs, xg_xs, xmem, xapu, AcpHal, XCRDAPI, XboxBvhBuilder, Bink2Scarlett

It is kept in cache/exe/ and is never committed.

docs.title: Harness
docs.text:
Tool What it does tools/pe_scan.py correct PE section mapping; proves negatives (sbox = 0 occurrences) tools/vtable_scan.py enumerates vtables, resolves a slot, finds which classes own an address cache/ghidra/Target.java decompile the function containing an address cache/ghidra/Refs.java references to an address, via Ghidra's reference manager cache/ghidra/Indirect.java indirect calls through a fixed structure displacement, from the instruction stream

Byte-pattern scans for call [reg+0x60] produce thousands of false hits; the instruction-stream version does not. Earlier scans also unpacked PE section fields in the wrong order and searched the wrong range — pe_scan.py exists so that "not found in .text" means what it says.

+0x38  section 1 base            p3 records of 8 bytes

Two facts come out of this that the corpus could not give:

  1. Buffer A is the arena header. The lookup code reads p3 and p5 straight out of the copied file bytes, so the fields at 0x1a/0x20 are the header, not a parallel structure.
  2. Section 1 is a u16-keyed table with a linear scan. 0x144e6f780 walks the records comparing a 16-bit key and returns 0xffff for "not found". A linear scan only makes sense for a small table, which matches p3 = 4..7 in the packs measured: section 1 is a dispatch table indexed by a small id, not a name hash table.

docs.title: The class map
docs.text:
vtable_scan.py --find 0x1462fd480 locates the archive vtable independently: 147 slots, and the two "create archive" factories are its own methods:

slot target role +0x018..+0x028 0x1428cd270, 2a0, 2e0 lifecycle +0x3a0 0x140fc2530 validity check used by the factory +0x3f8 0x1428ce0b0 key lookup (p5 path) +0x418 0x140fc2490 create child archive (constructor 1) +0x420 0x1411a8970 create child archive (constructor 2)

Because both factories are methods of the archive itself, archives nest: each RPF pack is mounted as its own archive over a bounded sub-stream of the parent. There is no external owner to find, which is why every reference search for one came up empty.

docs.title: The name hash, and why JOAAT was wrong
docs.text:
The archive's own name hash is Murmur3 x64-128, not JOAAT:

hash = murmur3_x64_128( tolower(name) with '\' -> '/' )

and the 16-bit id the archive indexes by is then looked up in a runtime table (FUN_14056ec70), so it cannot be computed from the string offline. JOAAT remains correct for object and field names in PSIN — a different subsystem — but every JOAAT-based attempt on archive entry names was aimed at the wrong function.

tools/name_hash_game.py implements the hash. Two things about it are now measured rather than believed:

  • The engine confirms it. Scanning the image for mov r64, imm64 whose immediate equals a recomputed hash finds 26 sites / 11 distinct names — trailers, graphics, snow, bird, train, discovery, none, null, default, dlc_ityp_request, permanent_ityp_file. A false match is expected 3 × 10⁻⁷ times, so these are real. tests/test_analysis_tools.py asserts one of them.
  • The metadata does not store them. 147,808 candidates against 3,716,607 front-region u64 words gives zero hits — consistent with the front region holding ids rather than hashes.

docs.title: What the executable rules out
docs.text: Claim Evidence the metadata is AES-encrypted zero occurrences of the forward S-box in the whole image; the single inverse S-box is CNG library code the metadata is decrypted by CNG only OpenAlgorithmProvider / GenRandom / CloseAlgorithmProvider are imported the front region is compressed zlib, raw deflate, lzma and bz2 all fail at the region start; the loader also copies rather than inflates the "CBC" reading of the front region identical plaintext prefixes explain the repeated-block statistic; there is no cipher call on the path

docs.title: Booting the console image under Wine
docs.text:
The image is a console build: its import table names xg_xs, d3d12_xs, xapu, xmem, AcpHal, XCRDAPI, XboxBvhBuilder and Bink2Scarlett, and the package carries gameos.xvd. Wine loads the PE, and each missing library is a single line in its log. A generator reads the import table and writes stub DLLs for the 117 console symbols plus one runtime module the image loads by name, xgameruntime.dll, which never appears in its import table.

Stop Call before it What the stop was 1 XMemVirtualAlloc(0, 0x600000000, …) CRT int 3 after initialisation returned 0x89240101 2 InitializeApiImplEx2 xgameruntime.dll absent 3 QueryApiImpl the out-slot is the third argument, not the second 4 GameInput!ordinal 1 the image imports GameInput by ordinal only 5 DStorageGetFactory the caller asserts on a null factory 6 — abort at game.exe+0x2237178, engine threads running

Six interfaces are then queried by GUID, and slot 2 of each is called as (object, buffer, 0x20). Filling those buffers with a repeated byte turns the abort into a stack overflow, which means the returned data reaches control flow: plausible bytes are not enough, the layouts are required.

That is the measured boundary. Passing it means implementing the memory, GPU and storage semantics of the platform, not more signatures — a project, not an iteration. The reproduction is one command (tools/rage.py play --stubs --game-dir <dump>), and the stub generator is tools/stub_dlls.py.

docs.title: What it still owes us
docs.text:
• the stream class behind Read (+0x60), which is the only link between the file and the copied bytes that has not been read;
  • the meaning of sections 2–5, which the layout sizes but does not describe;
  • the CHKS tag — ten 32-bit hash candidates are already excluded;
  • the script bytecode's container, which is not in a plaintext section.

Each of these is a code question with a known starting address, not a search problem. That is the difference the executable made.

docs.title: Hash names
docs.text:
Every identifier in the object graph, in bone tables and in weight arrays is JOAAT(lowercase(name)) — a 32-bit hash with no inverse. Names are recovered by vocabulary: hash candidate strings and keep the ones that collide with a value the game actually stores.

This is not the archive's entry-name hash. That one is Murmur3 x64-128 over a lower-cased name, and the 16-bit id it resolves to comes from a runtime dictionary — see the executable as a source. JOAAT names content; the other names files.

docs.title: Why confidence matters
docs.text:
A hash can be named by more than one source, and the sources disagree in two different ways:

  • case only — Position (engine metadata) against position (corpus). Same name, so the higher-confidence spelling wins and nothing is lost.
  • two real strings — ABON_YEA and CVA_WHEEL_REAR_LEFT really do share 0xbbb029a6. That is a JOAAT collision, not an error, and the registry marks the row ambiguous instead of pretending one is right.

Across the 267 hashes named by both the engine table and the corpus sweeps, 261 agree (98 %); the remaining 6 are collisions.

docs.title: RPF9 header
docs.text:
The loader reads 0x10 bytes, checks the magic, then mallocs the region and copies the header into it, so the first 0x10 bytes appear twice.

Offset Type Meaning Status +0x00 u32 magic 9FPR code +0x04 u32 size of buffer A → malloc argument code +0x08 u32 start offset of buffer B; +0x04 − +0x08 is its size code +0x0c u32 trailer length exact, 4,373/4,373 +0x10 u64 per-pack id measured, unique across all 654 headers in the local mirror +0x1a u16 arena field p3: count of 8-byte records code +0x1c u32 arena field p4: byte length of section 2 code +0x20 u16 arena field p5: count of 24-byte records; also [family][format] code +0x22 u16 arena field p6, subtracted from p5 code +0x24 u32 entry count N code +0x2c u8 arena field p8: 1 or 2, per-entry multiplier code +0x2d u8 flags; bit 0 selects 16-byte instead of 4-byte section alignment code +0x30 u32 +0x1c − 0x140 measured, 4,306/4,373

docs.title: Archive object (in memory)
docs.text:
+0x00  vtable 0x1462fd480 (147 slots)     +0x28  arena descriptor
+0x08  file / stream object               +0x30  pointer to buffer A (the header)
+0x18  buffer A base                      +0x38  section 1 (p3 x 8 bytes)
+0x20  buffer A size

The lookup code reads p3 from [+0x30]+0x1a and p5 from [+0x30]+0x20 — that is, straight out of the copied file header — and 0x144e6f780 scans the 8-byte records at +0x38 comparing a u16 key, returning 0xffff for "not found". So section 1 is a small u16-keyed dispatch table searched linearly, not a name hash table. Status: code.

docs.title: Buffer A: the arena
docs.text:
FUN_14087aff0 turns the header fields into five section offsets:

out[1] = align(base + 0x40)
out[2] = align(out[1] + p3 * 8)                    p3 records of 8 bytes
out[3] = align(out[2] + p4)                        p4 bytes
out[4] = align(out[3] + p5 * 0x18)                 p5 records of 24 bytes
out[5] = align8(out[4] + (p5 - p6) * N * p8)       (p5 - p6) * N * p8 bytes

For data.rpf+0 (p3=4, p4=336, p5=7, p6=1, N=699, p8=2) the sections land at 0x40..0x60, 0x60..0x1b0, 0x1b0..0x260, 0x260..0x2328.

The formula fits inside buffer A for 654 / 654 headers, which is what promotes the field offsets from guess to code.

Past out[5] sits a fifth region carrying N × a fixed per-pack size — exactly 64 in 79 packs, 112 in 21, 48 in 12, and otherwise 48–68 bytes per entry. Its bytes are high entropy (7.99) with no printable runs, so it is not a plaintext name blob in this build.

Status: code for the formula and exact for the fit; open for what each of the five regions contains.

docs.title: Buffer B: the entry table
docs.text:
A fixed-stride table, align16(N × stride). For mode family 0x0001 (2,908 of 4,373 headers) the stride is chosen by the +0x2c tag:

tag headers stride exact fits 0x00090f01 2,414 9 2,414 / 2,414 0x00090f02 494 10 494 / 494

Families 0x0002–0x0008 add a 16-aligned extra table S = size(B) − align16(stride × N), from 0 to 36,064 bytes.

Status: exact for family 1, open for the identity of S.

docs.title: Script metadata chain
docs.text:
script.rpf records are a chain of chunks, each [4-byte magic][big-endian u32: distance to the next chunk], emitted by FUN_144083410:

PSIN → LSCH → LENM → LSNS → LGID → LRSC → CHKS   (all seven, in every record)
Chunk Payload Status PSIN count × 16-byte {tag, length, 0xAA…} then each payload, rounded up to 16 code LSCH count rows of 32 bytes, then 16-byte sub-records code LENM count rows of 24 bytes, then 16-byte sub-records code LSNS opaque block of distance − 8 bytes code LGID u32 count then count × 16 bytes; empty when distance == 8 code LRSC fixed 0x50-byte block code CHKS u32 big-endian record size, then 4 unknown bytes exact, 60/60 size

The first PSIN payload starts at 16*count + 0x10 because the writer computes (16*count + 0x17) & ~15, which rounds down. count is not stored; it is the unique value that satisfies

16*count + 0x10 + Σ align16(length_i) == distance_to_next_chunk

Verified on the whole corpus: 1,012 / 1,012 records produce the complete chain.

docs.text:
Tag Role Records 0x85b4c631 typed rows 1,012 0xde396fe2 80-byte directory of five (count, count, kind, 0) entries 1,012 0x01393259 struct-like block with 0xffffffff sentinels 1,012 0x16 16-byte rows, 128-bit-looking material 1,010 0xaeb623d8 12-byte {u32, f32, f32} triples 855

docs.text:
+0x00  u32  property   164 distinct
+0x04  u32  key        14,530 distinct
+0x08  u32  value      role open: declaration index or reference
+0x0c  u32  type       0x101 int, 0x102 float, 0x103 hash, 0x104 bool, 0x105 byte

63,288 rows. The type word is last; an earlier reader used +0x04 and was 8 bytes misaligned, which paired every value with the next row's property. Status: code for the layout, open for value.

docs.text:
LSCH  32 bytes   +0x00 tag (one of this record's PSIN tags)  verified 200/200
                 +0x04 hash
                 +0x08 small
                 +0x10 u64 pointer, poisoned 0xAA on disk
                 +0x18 word  (matches block size only 36.7 % — a computed length)
                 +0x1e u16 sub-record count
LENM  24 bytes   +0x00 tag, +0x04 hash, +0x08 pointer (0xEE), +0x10 u16 count

Status: exact for the tag relation, open for the other fields. Of the 4,901 sections in the corpus, 3,891 are indexed by LSCH; the 1,010 that are not are exactly the 0x16 block, which the index never rows for.

docs.text:
+0x00  'KB2'   magic            +0x14  u32  width
+0x03  u8      version letter   +0x18  u32  height
+0x04  u32     payload size     +0x1c  u32  frames per second
+0x08  u32     frame count      ...
+0x10  u32     frame count, again

A container occupies align(0x800, payload size); validated against the distance to the next container. The duplicate frame count is the field that gave a false lead in restofworld before the KB2 magic was found.

docs.title: Audio (ADAT / AWC)
docs.text:
Header: ADAT, u16 version, u16 flags, u32 stream count, u32 header size — where the header size doubles as the data offset.

The stream table holds words id:29 | tag_count:3; the count is in the high three bits. The chunk table's position depends on the variant, but its shape does not: four records per stream (0x36 0x55 0x76 0xa3) and it ends exactly at the header size.

variant chunk table starts at status 0xff21 fixed 0x50 exact 0xff02 0x10 + 4·count exact 0xff61 longest valid 8-byte suffix before the header size measured 0xff25 same suffix scan measured

Record: type:8 | size:28 | offset:28. A bank ends at its furthest record, rounded up to 0x800. In audio.rpf these rules classify 99.687 % of 28.5 GB as 7,159 banks; the residual is the archive front region plus bytes that merely spell ADAT.

Streams decoded: 93,344 Opus + 1,818 XMA2 + 73 ACE1, zero failures. Status: exact for 0xff21/0xff02; measured for the suffix-scanned variants.

docs.title: RPF9 container format
docs.text: The observed archive begins with the little-endian magic bytes 9FPR (the ASCII spelling RPF9 is used throughout the code). The observed first header is 0x60 bytes. The code validates at least the first 0x40 bytes for payload operations. A pack has three metadata regions and a payload region.

docs.title: Byte layout
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    H["Header<br/>0x60 bytes"] --> A["Front A<br/>0x60 → word_08"]
    A --> B["Front B<br/>word_08 → word_04"]
    B --> P["Payload<br/>zlib chains · zero runs · opaque spans"]
    P --> T["Trailer<br/>end - word_0c → end"]

All four boundaries are 16-byte aligned in the observed samples. The header stores absolute archive offsets:

Word Offset Role Evidence word_04 +0x04 front_end end of Front B word_08 +0x08 Front A/B boundary align16(9N)/align16(10N) from it in mode family 1 word_0c +0x0c trailer byte length equals the trailer length in 4,373/4,373 headers word_24 +0x24 entry count N Front B law fits every family-1 header word_2c +0x2c entry format tag 2 values, split at N = 255/256 word_34..3c +0x34..+0x3c zero constant shared +0x40..+0x4c 16-byte constant block identical across all 4,373 headers profile +0x50..+0x5c profile block 4 values

Full word map, size laws, and masking evidence: Metadata regions.

docs.text: Front A, Front B, and the trailer are not decoded. They are 16-byte multiples, the trailer behaves CBC-like, and the size tables are measured. No key or plaintext name is recovered. See Metadata regions for the negative results and the exact wall.

docs.title: What the same two packs say about buffer B
docs.text:
pack word_08 .. word_04 per entry data.rpf+0 6,992 B 10.00 anim.rpf+0x94c000 32 B 10.67

Both are align16(N × stride) with stride 10 — the 0.67 is the 16-byte rounding on a 3-entry pack (3 × 10 = 30 → 32). The census over 4,373 headers fixes the stride at 9 or 10 depending on the +0x2c tag.

Buffer B is not a separate region. The loader allocates malloc(word_04) for the whole front region and, in its second mode, a second allocation for word_08 .. word_04 — a suffix of the first. So the entry table lives inside buffer A, at its end.

docs.text:
data.rpf pack 0, with pack_end taken from the next header (the last pack ends at the file size):

0x00000            header 0x40
0x00040 .. 0x11060 front region (buffer A; buffer B is its last 6,992 bytes)
0x11060 .. 0x68a790 payload window   6,788,912 bytes
0x68a790 .. 0x690000 trailer            22,640 bytes  (word_0c)
0x690000           next pack

The window is not a guess: measuring the union of the index ranges clipped to it gives 100 % coverage for every pack in every archive (tools/pack_extent_check.py).

One nuance, measured: 32 ranges cross a pack boundary and all of them are unclassified — 18 in data.rpf, 12 in textures.rpf, 2 in script.rpf. No classified payload (zlib, audio, zero-run, chain) ever crosses, which is what the model predicts: two packs are independent archives. The opaque spans are the partitioner's residual and simply do not know where a pack ends.

docs.title: Metadata regions
docs.text:
The metadata wall is the boundary between “the archive can be partitioned” and “the archive index can be decoded.”

The region sizes are modelled from the entry count, and the reading model is now taken from the executable rather than inferred: the loader copies the region verbatim and then interprets it through a 0x40-byte header that declares four sections. That changed the question from "what is the cipher" to "what are the four sections", and the census numbers below are retained because they still describe the bytes on disk.

The sizes and invariants below come from a census of 4,373 RPF9 headers across the 22-archive source tree (handoff/header-census-full.tsv, handoff/header-words.tsv).

docs.title: What the binary does
docs.text:
Two functions settle the reading model (FUN_141fb2600, FUN_14087aff0 in the analysed database):

read(stream, 0, .., buf16, 0x10)
if u32(buf16) == '9FPR':
    size = header[+4]                      ; or header[+8] in the second mode
    buf  = malloc(size)
    *buf = buf16 ; buf[1] = buf16[1]       ; the 16 header bytes are copied in
    read(stream, 0x10, buf + 0x10, size - 0x10)
    if mode == 1:
        size_b = header[+4] - header[+8]
        buf2   = malloc(size_b)
        read(stream, header[+8], buf2, size_b)

So both metadata buffers are plain copies of stream bytes, and the second one is not a separate region: it is file[word_08 .. word_04), which is the tail of the first buffer. There is no decryption call on this path.

Buffer A then starts with a 0x40-byte header whose fields drive an arena layout of four sections:

p3 = u16 @ 0x1a     p6 = u16 @ 0x22
p4 = u32 @ 0x1c     p7 = u32 @ 0x24   (the entry count N)
p5 = u16 @ 0x20     p8 = u8  @ 0x2c   (1 or 2)

out[1] = align(base + 0x40)
out[2] = align(out[1] + p3*8)                 ; p3 records of 8 bytes
out[3] = align(out[2] + p4)                   ; p4 bytes
out[4] = align(out[3] + p5*0x18)              ; p5 records of 24 bytes
out[5] = align8(out[4] + (p5-p6)*p7*p8)       ; (p5-p6) * N * p8 bytes

For data.rpf+0: p3=4, p4=336, p5=7, p6=1, p7=699, p8=2 — sections at 0x40..0x60, 0x60..0x1b0, 0x1b0..0x260, 0x260..0x2328. Everything from 0x2328 to the end of the buffer is not covered by the formula, so a fifth, variable region exists that the traced functions do not size.

This also explains a coincidence that misled the earlier write-up: "Front A starts at 0x60" is true only for packs whose first section happens to be 32 bytes.

docs.title: Front B size model
docs.text:
Front B is a fixed-stride entry table. For every header in mode family 0x0001 (2,908 of 4,373) the size is exactly align16(stride * N), where the stride is selected by the +0x2c tag:

+0x2c Headers Stride Exact fits 0x00090f01 2,414 9 bytes 2,414 / 2,414 0x00090f02 494 10 bytes 494 / 494

The tag is a count-driven format tag, not a build version: 0x00090f01 covers N = 1…254 and 0x00090f02 covers N = 257…27,172, with no overlap and no header at N = 255 or 256.

Because the law is align16(10N) exactly, the extra byte is inside every record, not a per-pack header byte (that would give align16(9N + c)). A per-record index running 0…N−1 fits a u8 up to N = 256 and forces the flip at N = 257; a per-record count running 1…N forces it at N = 256. Both readings survive because this build has no pack at either count.

Mode families 0x0002–0x0008 add a 16-byte-aligned extra table S = Front B − align16(stride * N). S is 0 for the smallest family-2 packs and grows to 36,064 bytes; family 4 is the tightest at 224 bytes per entry (±8), which points at a fixed-size per-entry descriptor. The localization cohort is the special case S = 2N + 12, which is why it also fits 12N + 12 and cannot distinguish the two readings on its own.

flowchart TD
    N[N entries] --> F{mode family}
    F -- "0x0001" --> T{"+0x2c tag"}
    T -- "0x00090f01" --> S9["align16(9N)"]
    T -- "0x00090f02" --> S10["align16(10N)"]
    F -- "0x0002..0x0008" --> SX["align16(stride*N) + S"]
    SX --> S["S: 16-aligned, 0 .. 36,064 B"]

docs.title: Entropy census (what the bytes look like)
docs.text:
For each header, the plug-in byte entropy of Front B was compared with the expected entropy of a uniform random sample of the same length (Monte Carlo below 1,000 bytes). The deficit is median 0.000, p75 0.009, max 0.357; only 64 of 4,373 regions exceed 0.15, and all are 16–80-byte samples where the statistic is coarse. All 4,373 first and all 4,373 last 16-byte blocks are distinct.

No pack in the corpus has a Front B table whose bytes look structured. That is a statement about appearance: the loader copies these bytes verbatim, so if a transform exists it is inside the stream's Read (+0x60), which is the one link in the chain not yet read. Uniform bytes are equally consistent with a dense pool of 64/128-bit hashes, which is why the entropy test alone cannot decide it — the 64-bit name-hash test in investigation.md is the sharper negative.

Cross-pack comparison is unavailable: across the thirteen data.rpf localization packs, which share N = 1,115 and a byte-identical 29,856-byte trailer, 0 of 13,392 Front B offsets are stable and byte agreement is at chance (tools/front_b_stability.py). The trailer chain is pack-independent; the Front B chain is not, or its plaintext is pack-specific in every record.

docs.title: Header word map
docs.text:
Offset Role Evidence +0x00 magic 9FPR constant +0x04 size of buffer A the loader passes it to malloc +0x08 start offset of buffer B the loader reads word_04 - word_08 bytes there +0x0c trailer byte length equals the trailer length in 4,373/4,373 +0x10, +0x14 per-pack id or salt unique per header +0x18 (k << 16) \| 0x7a00 k in {4,5,6,7,8}, tracks the mode family +0x1a arena p3: count of 8-byte records from FUN_14087aff0 +0x1c arena p4: byte length of section 2 from FUN_14087aff0 +0x20 arena p5: count of 24-byte records; also [u16 family][u16 format] 19 values +0x22 arena p6: subtracted from p5 from FUN_14087aff0 +0x24 entry count N (p7) the Front B law and the arena both use it +0x28 type hash 10 values, concentrated by mode +0x2c p8: 1 or 2, the per-entry multiplier 2 values, split exactly at N = 255/256 +0x2d flags, bit 0 selects 16-byte instead of 4-byte section alignment from FUN_14087aff0 +0x30 +0x1c − 0x140 4,306/4,373, exceptions are the k = 6 group +0x34, +0x38, +0x3c zero always zero +0x40..+0x4c constant 16-byte block one value across all headers +0x50..+0x5c profile block 4 values (2,906 / 1,398 / 67 / 2)

The thirteen data.rpf localization packs share a byte-identical 29,856-byte trailer and a single profile, but all thirteen buffer B bodies differ. Whatever the explanation, one of the two regions is language-independent and the other is not; the traced loader copies both verbatim, so any transform would sit in the stream's Read, which has not been read.

docs.text: This is the operational path from an RPF9 file to a report, a decoded stream, or a verified payload. The Rust CLI owns the byte-level gates; Python analysis consumes the results.

docs.title: End-to-end sequence
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant U as User
    participant CLI as rage-tools-vi
    participant A as Archive
    participant Z as zlib / flate2
    participant O as output
    participant P as Python tools

    U->>CLI: inspect archive
    CLI->>A: scan page-aligned 9FPR headers
    CLI-->>U: header table
    U->>CLI: packs / map / partition
    CLI->>A: read header words and payload
    CLI->>Z: verify each zlib stream
    Z-->>CLI: checksum-valid chunks
    CLI-->>U: spans and candidate entries
    U->>CLI: extract-zlib start end output
    CLI->>Z: decode aligned chain
    Z-->>CLI: decoded bytes
    CLI->>O: create-new output
    CLI-->>U: stream count and decoded size
    U->>P: parse report / decoded bytes
    P-->>U: names, arrays, tables

docs.title: Gate order
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    S[input bytes] --> M{starts with 9FPR?}
    M -- no --> E[error]
    M -- yes --> H[read header words]
    H --> B{front/trailer bounds valid?}
    B -- no --> E
    B -- yes --> P[payload range]
    P --> Z{16-byte-aligned zlib header?}
    Z -- no --> G[zero_run or unclassified span]
    Z -- yes --> C{checksum valid?}
    C -- no --> G
    C -- yes --> F{decoded == 64 KiB?}
    F -- yes --> N[next aligned offset; zero padding]
    N --> Z
    F -- no --> D[accept chain]
    D --> R[report span or write output]
    G --> R

docs.title: Continuation rule
docs.text:
A stream continues only when:

  1. the first decoded chunk is exactly 64 KiB;
  2. the next stream starts at the next 16-byte boundary after the previous stored stream;
  3. every byte in the intervening padding is zero;
  4. the final PSIN continuation has a valid CHKS section whose length matches the decoded total.
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> FirstStream
    FirstStream --> Short: decoded != 64 KiB
    FirstStream --> Full: decoded == 64 KiB
    Full --> Aligned: next multiple of 16
    Aligned --> Padded: all padding bytes zero
    Padded --> NextStream
    NextStream --> Short: final chunk
    NextStream --> Full: another full chunk
    Short --> [*]: accept and write
    Full --> [*]: reject unterminated chain
    Aligned --> [*]: bad padding

docs.title: Report → artifact
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    I[inspect] --> IH[header inventory]
    M[map] --> MS[span map]
    P[packs] --> PE[entropy / trailer bounds]
    D[partition] --> DC[candidate entries]
    S[sections] --> ST[section table]
    X[extract-zlib] --> OBJ[object bytes]
    OBJ --> PY[Python graph tools]
    PY --> TSV[handoff TSVs]
    IH --> DOC[plan / investigation]
    MS --> DOC
    PE --> DOC
    DC --> DOC
    ST --> DOC

docs.title: CLI examples
docs.text:
# Header inventory
target/debug/rage-tools-vi inspect script.rpf

# Partition and report the count comparison
target/debug/rage-tools-vi partition script.rpf

# Decode the 42-stream object
target/debug/rage-tools-vi extract-zlib \
  script.rpf 0x53000 0xc3b45 /tmp/object.bin

# Copy the parked blob literally
target/debug/rage-tools-vi extract-raw \
  script.rpf 0x2010 0x52fe0 /tmp/blob.bin

Exclusive ends and absolute offsets

Every start..end range is start-inclusive, end-exclusive, and absolute. Extraction refuses to overwrite an existing output path.
